c.tagline: Gulf trading capital of causeways, souqs, and skyline.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are standard for city taxis, but drivers often propose a flat rate for airport transfers or longer trips; confirm the price or insist on the meter before departing.

emergency.note: 999 is the single unified emergency number covering police, ambulance, and fire across Bahrain.

avoid.reason: Central Manama is safe, but avoid outlying villages such as Sanabis, Bani Jamra and Sitra if demonstrations flare, and steer clear of any political gathering.
Watch for taxi overcharging, be discreet with alcohol around the Juffair nightlife area late at night, and dress and behave conservatively during Ramadan.

hood_desc: Modern business and shopping district lined with malls, high-rise hotels, and the corniche; convenient and comfortable for travelers who want easy access to the financial district and dining.
Manama's arts and nightlife quarter (Block 338) packed with cafes, galleries, and restaurants; ideal for foodies and younger travelers wanting a walkable, buzzy base.
Expat-heavy strip lined with mid-range hotels, bars, and Western-style restaurants near the former US Navy base; popular with business travelers and weekend visitors from Saudi Arabia.
Manama's gleaming financial harbor of skyscrapers and 5-star hotels; suited to business travelers and luxury seekers who want waterfront views close to the old souq.
Man-made residential island with marinas, beaches, and resort hotels northeast of the city; best for families and travelers wanting a quieter, beach-oriented stay a taxi ride from downtown.
lodging: Ramada Hotel & Suites by Wyndham Amwaj Islands

water.note: Desalinated supply generally meets standards, but building plumbing varies; bottled water is a safe precaution.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the driver or via a prepaid Bahrain Bus smart card tapped on boarding. A light-rail/metro system (Bahrain Metro) is under construction but not yet operational as of 2026.
transit.hours: Buses generally run about 5:30am-11pm on main routes; frequency drops sharply at night and there is no true 24-hour service.
transit.note: Bahrain currently has no operating rail or metro; taxis and ride-hailing apps fill gaps outside bus routes and late hours.

bus: Bahrain Public Transport Company (BPTC) city buses
Intercity buses to Saudi Arabia via King Fahd Causeway

transit.m: Airport Bus route 20 to Manama city centre (~35 min)

tip.r: A ~10% service charge is often added at hotels and restaurants; extra tipping for good service is appreciated but not obligatory.

food.name: Machboos
food.desc: Bahrain's national dish: spiced basmati rice slow-cooked with chicken, lamb or fish, loomi (dried lime), baharat and caramelised onion.

places.name: Emmawash Traditional Restaurant
places.note: Big-portion Bahraini and Khaleeji home cooking at low prices; a reliable first machboos.

places.name: Saffron by Jena
places.note: Award-winning local chef reworking Bahraini classics; good vegetarian versions too.

food.name: Muhammar with fried safi
food.desc: Sweet date-syrup rice served alongside fried safi (rabbitfish), the classic Bahraini sweet-and-salty seafood pairing.

places.name: Haji's Traditional Cafe
places.note: Serving the old souq since the 1950s; communal tables and unfussy Bahraini plates.

places.name: Machaabees
places.note: Local favourite for rice-and-fish platters; order the fish of the day off the counter.

food.name: Balaleet
food.desc: Breakfast of sweet cardamom-and-saffron vermicelli topped with a thin savoury omelette, eaten across the Gulf but perfected in Bahrain.

places.name: Haji's Traditional Cafe
places.note: Go early; the balaleet and foul breakfast is the whole reason people queue.

places.name: Emmawash Traditional Restaurant
places.note: Balaleet and baid tamat served all day, with fresh khubz baked on site.

food.name: Samboosa
food.desc: Crisp fried triangles stuffed with spiced mince, cheese or vegetables; a street snack that takes over Manama in Ramadan.

places.name: Manama Souq food carts
places.note: Wooden carts fry them to order in the lanes off Bab Al Bahrain, cheapest and freshest.

places.name: Al Abraaj
places.note: Busy Bahraini-Lebanese grill house; samboosa and mezze before the mixed grills.

food.name: Bahraini halwa
food.desc: Translucent saffron-and-cardamom starch pudding studded with nuts, stirred in copper vats and offered to every guest as a mark of welcome.

places.name: Showaiter Sweets
places.note: The Showaiter family has made this halwa for generations; the benchmark version.

places.name: Halwa shops of Manama Souq
places.note: Several old-school makers sell by weight; ask for a warm sample before buying.

food.name: Ghoozi
food.desc: Whole slow-roasted lamb over spiced rice with nuts and raisins, the celebration platter Bahraini families order for a crowd.

places.name: Al Abraaj
places.note: Long-running local institution; generous grills and lamb platters, family-friendly.

places.name: Emmawash Traditional Restaurant
places.note: Traditional Khaleeji roasts at everyday prices; best shared between three or four.

food.name: Karak chai
food.desc: Strong black tea boiled with evaporated milk, cardamom and plenty of sugar, poured into small glasses at every hour of the day.

places.name: Haji's Traditional Cafe
places.note: Chai haleeb from the same pot locals have been drinking for decades.

places.name: Souq Al Qaysariya cafes
places.note: Restored coffee-house lane; sit outside with karak and watch the souq trade.

food.name: Gahwa
food.desc: Pale Arabic coffee scented with cardamom and saffron, poured from a dallah into thimble cups and served with dates, never sweetened.

places.name: Saffron by Jena
places.note: Proper dallah service with Bahraini dates and halwa alongside.

places.name: Bahrain Fort visitor cafe
places.note: Gahwa and dates with a view over the Qal'at al-Bahrain ruins and the sea.

landmarks: Bahrain World Trade Center
This twin sail-shaped skyscraper was the first in the world to integrate large-scale wind turbines directly into its design, symbolizing modern Bahrain.
Al Fateh Grand Mosque
One of the world's largest mosques, its gleaming white dome and vast marble interior welcome visitors of all faiths to explore Islamic art and architecture.
Bahrain Fort (Qal'at al-Bahrain)
This UNESCO World Heritage archaeological mound reveals 4,000 years of layered civilizations, capped by a restored Portuguese-era fort overlooking the Gulf.
Bahrain National Museum
The country's largest and oldest museum traces Bahrain's history from ancient Dilmun burial mounds to modern traditions in striking waterfront galleries.
Bab Al Bahrain
This iconic gateway building, built in 1949, marks the entrance to Manama Souq and remains a beloved symbol of the capital's colonial-era history.
Manama Souq
A maze of bustling lanes selling gold, spices, textiles, and souvenirs, this traditional market captures the sensory energy of old Manama.
Arad Fort
A beautifully restored 15th-century coral-stone fort near the causeway, especially photogenic when illuminated against the night sky.
Isa Cultural Centre
A striking modern complex blending Islamic architectural motifs, home to exhibitions, a library, and cultural events celebrating Bahraini heritage.
Manama Skyline
The glittering waterfront panorama of glass towers and the Bahrain World Trade Center makes for one of the Gulf's most photographed cityscapes.
Al Fateh Corniche & Bahrain Bay
A scenic waterfront promenade offering relaxed walks with views of Manama's modern skyline reflected in the calm Gulf waters.

train.note: Bahrain has no railway. A national metro and a GCC cross-border rail link are planned but not yet open. The nearest trains are in Saudi Arabia (Dammam), reached by causeway bus.

bus.note: International coaches cross the King Fahd Causeway to Saudi Arabia. Carry your passport and a valid Saudi visa; border formalities are done at the causeway checkpoints.

ferry.note: There are no scheduled international passenger ferries from Bahrain. Local boats serve leisure trips to the Hawar Islands but do not cross borders.

half.name: Qal'at al-Bahrain (Bahrain Fort)
half.blurb: A UNESCO site where an ancient fort crowns layers of the old Dilmun capital.

half.name: Tree of Life
half.blurb: A lone centuries-old tree thriving in the desert draws curious visitors from across the island.

half.name: Al Areen Wildlife Park
half.blurb: A nature reserve where visitors spot oryx, gazelles and other Arabian wildlife up close.

half.name: Bahrain International Circuit
half.blurb: The Formula One racetrack offers tours and karting for motorsport fans in the desert.

half.name: Muharraq
half.blurb: The old capital charms with traditional houses, Arad Fort and the pearling trail heritage.

half.name: Hawar Islands
half.blurb: A remote archipelago prized for birdlife, dugongs and quiet, unspoiled beaches.
